projects.title: Kiwi Swerve Drivetrain
projects.summary: A low-power, affordable three-module omnidirectional drivetrain built for competition and teaching.

overview.problem: Competition swerve drives often demand four power-hungry modules, specialized parts, and a budget that puts omnidirectional motion out of reach for smaller teams.
overview.method: I reduced the drivetrain to three steerable pods, selected readily available hardware, and shifted steering accuracy into encoder-based Python control on a Raspberry Pi.
overview.result: The first robot validated a lower-cost, lower-power architecture with full-direction movement and created a practical platform for a more refined second version.

sections.heading: First Robot
sections.body: This first prototype established the low-cost, three-module Kiwi swerve concept and provided the foundation for the next version.

sections.heading: Overview
sections.body: The Kiwi swerve drivetrain is a low-power, affordable, and easy-to-maintain omnidirectional drive system for robotics competitions and real-world robotic applications. Using three modules instead of four, continuous-rotation servos with encoder feedback, and general-purpose mechanical components reduces cost and complexity while maintaining smooth, capable motion. A custom electronics stack and Python control system replace expensive hardware solutions and make the platform practical for teaching robotics design and programming.

sections.heading: First Prototype — Build
sections.body: The first prototype uses general-purpose gears and bearings sourced from Amazon and ServoCity, making its pods less expensive and easier to replace. Its structure combines 3D-printed parts, CNC-machined plates, and standard hardware. Each module uses a continuous-rotation servo with an encoder for closed-loop steering; an HTD5 belt connects the servo to the pod. The drive motor uses a longer, lighter HTD2 belt, allowing the motor and steering servo to remain stationary while the pod turns freely.

sections.heading: Electronics
sections.body: A Raspberry Pi anchors the custom electronics stack. Each drive motor is powered by a 10-amp motor driver, steering is managed through a servo HAT, and a 12-bit encoder board provides precise steering-angle feedback for every module. These generic, maintainable components keep the system accessible and easy to modify.

sections.heading: Programming
sections.body: Python software running on the Raspberry Pi implements Kiwi swerve kinematics, translating driver or autonomous commands into coordinated three-module motion. Closed-loop steering continuously compares encoder feedback with the target angle, correcting the continuous-rotation servos in real time for smooth, predictable movement. The software also synchronizes steering and drive motion to keep modules aligned and minimize unnecessary power draw.

sections.heading: Second Robot — V2 in Progress
sections.body: The second Kiwi swerve robot is currently in development. This next version will build on the first prototype’s mechanical design, electronics, and software control system.

projects.title: A-Eye Animatronic Chatbot
projects.summary: A voice-activated AI assistant that combines real-time conversation with a smooth, expressive animatronic eye.

overview.problem: Voice assistants can sound responsive while still feeling physically disconnected, and adding moving hardware introduces noise that can disrupt listening.
overview.method: I paired a compact two-axis eye and linked eyelids with conversational software, then coordinated motion and microphone states so expression never competed with speech input.
overview.result: The prototype responds as both a conversational system and an expressive object, with natural-looking motion that remains quiet enough for dependable interaction.

sections.heading: Challenge
sections.body: The goal was to create a lifelike, voice-activated assistant that could listen and respond naturally while controlling an expressive mechanical eye without servo noise interfering with speech recognition.

sections.heading: Mechanical Design
sections.body: Two hidden servos move the eye vertically and horizontally from a compact mechanism mounted to a monitor arm. Linked upper and lower eyelids create synchronized expressions, while reinforced pivots keep the movement stable and repeatable.

sections.heading: Controls
sections.body: The software combines wake-word detection, speech recognition, and ChatGPT conversation. Cosine easing smooths eye and eyelid movement, coordinated states manage blinking and attention, and the servos pause while the microphone is listening to reduce noise.

sections.heading: Result
sections.body: The completed prototype can wake, listen, converse, interrupt, and reset in real time. Smooth eye motion and synchronized blinking give the assistant a more natural presence while preserving reliable voice interaction.

projects.title: Coaxial Swerve Drive
projects.summary: A compact FTC swerve module redesigned around accessible parts, a small footprint, and broad hardware compatibility.

overview.problem: Most FTC-scale swerve modules are difficult to package, expensive to reproduce, and tied to a narrow set of proprietary components.
overview.method: I built and compared two compact coaxial pod designs, using the first to prove the geometry and the second to prioritize common parts and multiple mounting standards.
overview.result: The redesign retained the compact steering concept while lowering the barrier to repair, replacement, and adoption by teams using different hardware ecosystems.

sections.heading: Challenge
sections.body: Traditional FTC swerve modules can be too large and expensive for many teams. This project explored a compact, maintainable coaxial pod that could fit inside a competition robot without requiring specialized components.

sections.heading: First Prototype
sections.body: The first design fit inside a four-inch cube and combined a printed structure with shafts, gears, and bearings. A four-pod drivetrain used one motor and one servo per module, proving the steering and drive arrangement worked as a complete chassis.

sections.heading: Second Prototype
sections.body: The follow-up version replaced expensive specialty hardware with generic Amazon and AliExpress parts. Its shape changed from an L-shaped module to a rectangular pod, added mounting support for GoBilda, REV, and AndyMark systems, and grew by less than a quarter inch.

sections.heading: Result
sections.body: The first pod worked but cost about $350, putting the full chassis near $1,300. The second design substantially reduced cost while improving compatibility and serviceability, creating a stronger foundation for continued development.

projects.title: Simple Swerve Drive
projects.summary: A cost-conscious differential swerve chassis engineered to fit FTC size rules and common team hardware.

overview.problem: Differential swerve offers unusual mobility, but its gearing, size, and component count make it a difficult off-season experiment within FTC constraints.
overview.method: I simplified a proven differential layout, embedded bearings directly in the gears, and repeatedly repackaged the motors until the chassis fit the legal envelope.
overview.result: The project is complete. It produced an adaptable two-pod foundation with locally preserved CAD releases for REV and GoBILDA hardware.

sections.heading: Challenge
sections.body: After the 2023-2024 NYC FTC championship, the goal was to build an off-season swerve robot despite the complexity, packaging constraints, and cost that make swerve uncommon in FTC.

sections.heading: Development
sections.body: The design began with a study of differential swerve and a simplified version of FTC 11115's approach. The gearbox was reengineered around M3x45 bolts and bearings embedded in the gears, reducing specialized hardware while preserving the core mechanism.

sections.heading: Chassis Iteration
sections.body: The first layout measured 18.25 inches, so the motors were rotated 90 degrees with REV Ultra 90 gearboxes to meet FTC sizing. A two-pod chassis used omni wheels at the other corners and included space for a slide mechanism. Version two added lower-cost configurations for REV Ultraplanetary and GoBilda Yellow Jacket motors.

sections.heading: Result
sections.body: The project is complete. The repository now preserves the full explanation, development images, and four downloadable CAD packages without depending on the former portfolio page or GrabCAD.

projects.title: FTC 9384 Robot: EggWUUUHH
projects.summary: Team 9384's four-iteration CENTERSTAGE robot, built to score pixels, launch a plane, and climb reliably.

overview.problem: CENTERSTAGE combined intake, precise backdrop scoring, launching, and climbing in one robot, leaving little room for a mechanism that could not evolve during the season.
overview.method: Our team treated the machine as a sequence of testable subsystems and revised the chassis, lift, intake, outtake, and endgame hardware as match feedback exposed weaknesses.
overview.result: Four revisions converged on a competition-ready robot whose systems were reliable enough to perform the full game cycle and document a clear iteration story.

sections.heading: Challenge
sections.body: The CENTERSTAGE season required one robot to collect and score pixels on the backdrop, launch a paper plane, and climb at the end of a match. The team needed a design that could evolve rapidly throughout the season.

sections.heading: Core Systems
sections.body: The robot used a custom aluminum-sheet mecanum chassis, stacked drawer-slide lift with printed spacers and pulleys, and a three-stage active intake. The backdrop outtake evolved through multiple pivot and pincher designs as testing exposed alignment and reliability issues.

sections.heading: Endgame and Autonomous
sections.body: A spring-powered plane launcher handled the season's launch task, while an autonomous pixel pincher improved repeatable placement. The final climbing system paired a winch with pivoting hooks and passive rubber assistance.

sections.heading: Result
sections.body: Across four major revisions, the team produced a reliable competition platform with strong slide, intake, outtake, launcher, and climber systems. The complete CAD and engineering portfolio document the full iteration process.

projects.title: Tubba Odometry Pods
projects.summary: A competition-proven dead-wheel tracking system designed before compact FTC odometry pods were widely available off the shelf.

overview.problem: We wanted dependable live robot-position tracking for autonomous routines and driver assistance at a time when compact FTC odometry pods were not yet a common off-the-shelf option. Existing approaches were expensive, difficult to package, or left teams to build the mechanism themselves.
overview.method: I designed a compact dead-wheel pod around the essential tracking system: a passive 2-inch omni wheel coupled to a through-bore encoder. The plates, shaft support, preload, mounting geometry, and robot integration were developed specifically for Team 9384's chassis, then calibrated as part of the localization system.
overview.result: The completed pods were installed on EggWUUUHH and used successfully in competition. They tracked the robot consistently, strengthened autonomous path accuracy, and provided position feedback that could also support corrections during teleop driving.

sections.heading: Challenge
sections.body: Reliable odometry required far more than attaching an encoder to a wheel. The complete module had to fit inside the robot, maintain dependable contact with the field, minimize sideways scrub, protect the sensor, and return repeatable measurements through impacts, fast direction changes, and an entire competition match.

sections.heading: Core System
sections.body: At its center, each pod used a REV through-bore encoder and a passive 2-inch AndyMark Dualie omni wheel. The tracking wheel rotated independently from the drivetrain, allowing the localization software to measure the robot's actual movement instead of estimating position only from powered-wheel motion and slip.

sections.heading: Designed From Scratch
sections.body: Because a ready-made solution was not available for our requirements, I designed the plates, shaft arrangement, bearings, wheel support, preload system, and chassis mounting as one compact assembly. The finished pod fit within EggWUUUHH's parallel-plate structure and was documented as a complete STEP assembly with individual manufacturing files.

sections.heading: Cost and Accessibility
sections.body: A pod cost roughly $100 in 2024, which was an affordable result for custom competition-grade localization hardware at the time. The encoder represented the largest share of the early prototype budget; the rest of the mechanism used a printed structure, a standard omni wheel, common bearings, shaft stock, tubing, and ordinary fasteners to keep the design serviceable and reproducible.

sections.heading: Competition Result
sections.body: The system was installed, calibrated, and run on our competition robot with strong results. Its live position estimate made autonomous motion more repeatable and gave the control system useful feedback for correcting movement during teleop. The project turned a sensor and tracking wheel into a compact, field-tested localization tool that the team could actually trust in a match.

projects.title: FTC 9384 Robot: Crabby
projects.summary: Team 9384's POWERPLAY robot, refined through three designs for faster cone scoring and a more stable chassis.

overview.problem: POWERPLAY rewarded rapid cone cycles at several heights, so lift speed, turret accuracy, and drivetrain rigidity all had to improve together.
overview.method: We rebuilt the robot through three major configurations, replacing flexible or slow mechanisms with rigid slides, a claw, reinforced structure, and a more capable turret.
overview.result: The final revision delivered a lower, sturdier scoring platform and turned competition observations into concrete mechanical gains across the whole machine.

sections.heading: Challenge
sections.body: POWERPLAY required the robot to collect cones and place them on junction poles at several heights. Fast cycling, accurate alignment, and chassis stability were all critical to competitive performance.

sections.heading: Early Designs
sections.body: The first version paired REV linear slides with an H-pattern mecanum chassis and a dual compliant-wheel intake. Later iterations increased lift speed, replaced the roller intake with a claw, and introduced a direct-drive turret supported by a lazy susan bearing.

sections.heading: Final Revision
sections.body: The final robot used dual rigid slides, an internal bevel-gearbox chassis, a larger turret, and a reinforced frame. These changes addressed flex, speed, and alignment problems found during competition testing.

sections.heading: Result
sections.body: Three major design cycles produced a polished FTC machine with a stable low-profile drivetrain, fast lift, reliable claw, and precise turret. The project provided direct experience turning match feedback into mechanical improvements.

projects.title: ZeroG Hydra 3D Printer
projects.summary: A large-format CoreXY printer focused on print quality, automatic calibration, sensing, and robust hardware.

overview.problem: Large-format printers often trade consistency and serviceability for build volume or headline speed, especially when calibration still depends on manual adjustment.
overview.method: I centered the design on a rigid CoreXY frame, three-point automated bed alignment, modular electronics, and a sensor-rich toolhead built around repeatable extrusion.
overview.result: The in-progress Hydra now serves as a quality-first flagship platform, with the core motion, calibration, and monitoring architecture established for continued development.

sections.heading: Challenge
sections.body: After building and modifying several printers, the goal was a large-volume machine that prioritized print quality, robust hardware, and sensor-driven reliability instead of chasing speed alone.

sections.heading: Motion and Bed
sections.body: The Hydra uses a CoreXY motion system and a three-point, independently pivoting floating bed. Each point can adjust during automatic tramming, creating a rigid platform while letting the firmware correct alignment before a print.

sections.heading: Electronics and Toolhead
sections.body: An under-printer electronics bay houses the USB hub, controller, power supply, solid-state relay for the 110-volt bed, and the Linux computer running Klipper. The Filimetrix-inspired toolhead adds dual filament sensors, a cutter, Beacon eddy-current probing, lighting, a touchscreen, a Phaetus Rapido hotend, and a Clockwork 2 extruder.

sections.heading: Status
sections.body: The printer remains in development, but its large build volume, automated calibration, sensor-rich toolhead, and high-quality extrusion system establish it as a flagship quality-focused machine.

projects.title: Delta 3D Printer
projects.summary: A high-speed delta printer rebuilt around closed-loop motion, direct-drive extrusion, and powerful CPAP cooling.

overview.problem: The delta frame could move quickly, but friction, cooling limitations, and difficult calibration kept that speed from producing consistently clean parts.
overview.method: I converted the machine through several toolhead generations, moving to direct drive, closed-loop motion, stronger remote cooling, and a nozzle-based probing strategy.
overview.result: The rebuilt printer combines delta speed with dependable extrusion and calibration, producing repeatable parts without the artifacts that limited the original setup.

sections.heading: Challenge
sections.body: The project set out to combine delta-printer speed with consistent print quality, using closed-loop stepper motors, a lightweight effector, and strong part cooling while working through the calibration and packaging challenges unique to delta kinematics.

sections.heading: Development
sections.body: The TEVO Little Monster frame, power supply, and solid-state relay became the foundation. An early Bowden setup introduced friction and surface artifacts, so later revisions moved to direct drive and a frame-mounted CPAP blower feeding the effector through a lightweight hose.

sections.heading: Toolhead Iterations
sections.body: Version two combined ducts, hotend, extruder, and probe but exposed airflow and probe-offset problems. Version three lowered the hotend and center of gravity, improved the ducts, and added a detachable nozzle probe. Closed-loop NEMA 17 motors with encoders and a TFT35 KlipperScreen completed the control system.

sections.heading: Result
sections.body: The finished machine prints quickly and consistently, pairing reliable closed-loop motion with high-flow direct-drive extrusion, improved calibration, strong cooling, and a custom user interface.

projects.title: Voron V0.2990
projects.summary: A heavily modified compact Voron built for higher flow, better cooling, safer operation, and easier servicing.

overview.problem: The compact Voron platform was capable, but heat management, extrusion flow, monitoring, and access to electronics limited long-term speed and reliability.
overview.method: I upgraded the machine as one integrated system, pairing a higher-flow toolhead with external cooling, enclosure sensing, filtration, failure monitoring, and service-friendly wiring.
overview.result: The finished modifications make the small printer faster to run, easier to maintain, and safer to leave working through demanding high-speed jobs.

sections.heading: Challenge
sections.body: Starting from the community-designed Voron platform, this build focused on identifying performance bottlenecks and improving extrusion, cooling, monitoring, filtration, and service access.

sections.heading: Performance Upgrades
sections.body: A custom toolhead combines a stronger extruder and high-flow hotend for printing around 225-350 mm/s with travel speeds up to 650 mm/s. An external 12032 fan increases part cooling without adding excessive moving mass.

sections.heading: Reliability and Usability
sections.body: The enclosure adds active carbon filtration, a chamber thermistor, RGB-lit reinforced panels, upgraded hinges, and a camera for failure detection and timelapses. A filament runout and extrusion sensor monitors material flow, while a larger Mini12864 display improves local control.

sections.heading: Serviceability
sections.body: DIN-rail electronics, a hinged rear electronics door, and a quiet Noctua cooling fan make maintenance and thermal management easier. Together, the modifications turn the compact printer into a faster, safer, and more dependable machine.

projects.title: Self-Balancing Robot
projects.summary: Three low-cost balancing robots built from school parts to teach feedback control across Raspberry Pi and Arduino platforms.

sections.heading: Challenge
sections.body: The club wanted a practical controls project that could be built with parts already available at school. A self-balancing robot made gyroscope feedback, tuning, and real-time motor control visible and easy to experiment with.

sections.heading: Build
sections.body: Three robots were created: one controlled by a Raspberry Pi running Python and two based on Arduino Nano and Uno boards. Each used an existing motor driver, DC motors, and gyroscope inside a custom chassis.

sections.heading: Controls
sections.body: A closed-loop PID controller processes the robot angle, synchronizes both motors, and corrects disturbances. Repeated PID tuning and changes to wheel placement, chassis geometry, and center of gravity improved stability across each platform.

sections.heading: Result
sections.body: All three robots can balance while stationary and moving forward or backward. The low-cost platforms turned PID control, embedded programming, and mechanical tradeoffs into an expandable hands-on teaching system.

projects.title: Crab Crawler
projects.summary: A trio of compact ESP32 walking robots designed to teach wireless programming, sensors, and coordinated servo motion.

sections.heading: Challenge
sections.body: The project needed to introduce ESP32 programming, camera feedback, sensors, and servo breakout boards through a robot simple enough for students to understand and modify.

sections.heading: Build
sections.body: Three compact crawlers were assembled from 3D-printed frames, two servos per robot, an ESP32-CAM for wireless control and video, an OLED status display, and a dedicated servo driver.

sections.heading: Programming
sections.body: Custom code coordinates the walking gait, live display information, camera connection, and wireless commands. The gait and body geometry were tuned together to improve traction and keep the two-servo mechanism stable.

sections.heading: Result
sections.body: The crawlers walk reliably, stream live feedback, and report status in real time. Their low part count and expandable code make them an approachable educational platform for embedded robotics.

projects.title: AutoCAD Coursework
projects.summary: Freshman drafting coursework spanning dimensioned 2D drawings, layer organization, and 3D solid modeling.

sections.heading: Coursework
sections.body: Two freshman AutoCAD courses covered the transition from precise 2D drafting to three-dimensional solid modeling. Assignments emphasized correct dimensions, readable layouts, layer organization, and clean geometric construction.

sections.heading: Skills Developed
sections.body: The work strengthened drafting fundamentals and the ability to communicate a part through both orthographic drawings and finished 3D geometry. Repeated exercises improved speed, accuracy, and consistency inside a professional CAD workflow.

sections.heading: Archive
sections.body: The linked coursework folder contains selected drawings and models from both classes.

projects.title: Mastercam Coursework
projects.summary: CAM coursework connecting CAD models to CNC machining through practical toolpaths, feeds, speeds, and tooling choices.

sections.heading: Coursework
sections.body: This freshman course began with existing CAD experience and introduced the manufacturing decisions required to turn a digital model into CNC machine instructions.

sections.heading: Process
sections.body: Projects covered 2D and 3D machining strategies, toolpath creation, stock setup, feeds and speeds, tool selection, and simulation. Each assignment connected model geometry to the physical sequence a mill would follow.

sections.heading: Result
sections.body: The course built a practical understanding of the full CAD-to-CAM workflow and how design choices affect machining time, tool access, surface finish, and manufacturability.

projects.title: MATLAB Coursework
projects.summary: Programming coursework applying scripts, functions, matrices, and data visualization to mathematical and engineering problems.

sections.heading: Coursework
sections.body: This freshman course extended a foundation in basic Python into MATLAB's engineering-focused programming environment. Assignments introduced a different syntax and a workflow built around numerical problem solving.

sections.heading: Computing Skills
sections.body: Projects used scripts and reusable functions to work with matrices, arrays, and structured calculations. Built-in numerical tools made it possible to analyze data and test mathematical relationships efficiently.

sections.heading: Application
sections.body: Plots and visualizations turned computed results into readable engineering evidence. The course connected programming with the mathematical models and data interpretation used throughout engineering work.

projects.title: CUNY Research: 3D Printing With Geopolymers
projects.summary: Summer 2025 research developing lower-impact geopolymer materials and a custom printer capable of extruding them.

sections.heading: Research
sections.body: During Summer 2025 at New York City College of Technology, the project explored eco-friendly geopolymer mixtures as a printable construction material. Work included material formulation, curing studies, structural evaluation, and iterative extrusion testing.

sections.heading: Printer Development
sections.body: A custom 3D printer was designed and built to handle the material, joining mechanical design with experiments in flow, consistency, layer formation, and process control.

sections.heading: Recognition
sections.body: The work was presented at CUNY's Third Annual Celebrating Research Excellence Symposium and earned a Certificate of Research Achievement for completing and presenting two summer research projects.

projects.title: NSF Advanced Manufacturing Training
projects.summary: A five-week manufacturing program covering microscopy, CNC machining, additive manufacturing, CAD, and technical communication.

sections.heading: Program
sections.body: During freshman year, this five-week NSF Advanced Manufacturing Summer Training Camp introduced a broad range of equipment and professional engineering practices.

sections.heading: Technical Experience
sections.body: Hands-on work included electron microscopes, CNC mills, 3D printers, SolidWorks, and Autodesk Inventor. The program connected inspection, modeling, machining, and additive manufacturing inside one production workflow.

sections.heading: Communication
sections.body: Weekly video updates and presentations developed the ability to document technical work, explain decisions, and communicate progress in an industry-style format.
